s: Use your ChatGPT or Claude subscription
x: Use your ChatGPT or Claude subscription OpenAI and Anthropic set different rules for other apps, so the two work differently. Here is exactly what to do, and what happens. ChatGPT plan For ChatGPT Plus and Pro, and Codex users. werkz uses OpenAI's official Sign in with ChatGPT; it doesn't use the Codex app or its login. In werkz, type /login chatgpt . Your browser opens; choose Continue with ChatGPT . Type /model and pick a model marked plan . The status bar shows Using ChatGPT plan . Requests count toward your plan's limits, the same ones Codex uses. Over SSH, werkz prints the link and the port to forward. OpenAI doesn't share plan usage with apps, so /usage shows it only when ChatGPT reports it; see chatgpt.com/settings/usage . /logout chatgpt signs out. Claude subscription For Claude Pro and Max. Anthropic doesn't let other apps sign in with a Claude account, so werkz runs your own Claude Code , which uses its own login. Install Claude Code , run claude in a terminal and sign in with /login . werkz never sees this login. In werkz, type /model and pick a model marked (Claude Code) . Claude Code does the work; werkz shows every step and asks you before anything risky, with its usual rules. werkz lends it its browser, dev servers and your MCP tools, so you can watch it work on a page with /browser view . The status bar and /usage show your 5-hour and weekly limits, and a model's own weekly limit such as Fable, with when each resets. If werkz says Claude Code isn't signed in, run claude and /login again.

Nothing risky without asking Press Shift + Tab to choose how much werkz may do on its own. Bypass, the one that asks for nothing, lasts only for the current session. Anything outside your working folders asks first, in every mode except Bypass. Credential locations such as ~/.ssh and ~/.aws are never opened, in any mode. Your code goes only to the provider you chose. No werkz server, no telemetry. Fewer tokens, by design Long coding sessions re-send the whole conversation with every request. werkz makes that cheap without you managing it. Prompt caching Follow-up requests read 97–99% of their input from Claude's prompt cache, which werkz keeps warm while you think. Compaction At 300k tokens by default, werkz replaces a long conversation with a structured summary; /compact does it on demand. Your own context window /context window 350k caps the window for every model, and werkz keeps the conversation inside it. Trimmed output Long test and build output is trimmed to what matters, with the full text saved to a file the model can read if it needs to.

Start in a minute Install werkz, open a project folder and type werkz . Paste any key you have, sign in with ChatGPT, or press Esc to use a local model. It runs on Linux (x86-64, ARM64) and macOS (Apple Silicon, Intel), and every release is signed and checksummed. curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/TonmoyTalukder/werkz/main/install.sh | sh The script downloads the latest release for your system from GitHub Releases , checks its SHA-256 checksum, and installs: Linux: the werkz command in ~/.local/bin , plus a werkz icon in your app grid and on your Desktop. Set WERKZ_NO_DESKTOP=1 to install only the command. macOS: werkz.app in /Applications (or ~/Applications if that isn't writable), plus a werkz command in ~/.local/bin . To install a specific version: curl -fsSL …/install.sh | WERKZ_VERSION=v0.1.0 sh . If ~/.local/bin isn't on your PATH , the installer tells you; add this to your shell profile: export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"

Every release has these files: File For werkz-<version>-linux.tar.gz Linux package: both architectures, installer, launcher and icons werkz-<version>-macos.zip macOS: werkz.app for Apple Silicon and Intel werkz-<version>-linux-amd64 , -linux-arm64 , -darwin-amd64 , -darwin-arm64 The bare command for one system SHA256SUMS Checksums for all of the above Linux package: tar xzf werkz-0.1.0-linux.tar.gz cd werkz-linux && ./install.sh The installer adds the command, an app-grid entry and a Desktop icon. If the Desktop icon shows as a plain file, right-click it and choose Allow Launching . Clicking it opens werkz in a new terminal window (ptyxis, GNOME Terminal, Konsole, kitty, Alacritty, WezTerm, foot, Tilix or xterm, whichever is installed); set WERKZ_TERMINAL=kitty to choose one. macOS app: unzip werkz-0.1.0-macos.zip and drag werkz.app to Applications. The app isn't signed with an Apple Developer ID, so the first time you open a browser-downloaded copy, right-click it and choose Open , or run: xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine /Applications/werkz.app macOS also asks once for permission for werkz to control Terminal. (The one-line installer downloads with curl , which doesn't set the quarantine flag.) A bare binary: download the one for your system, then: chmod +x werkz-0.1.0-linux-amd64 mv werkz-0.1.0-linux-amd64 ~/.local/bin/werkz Verify any download with sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS --ignore-missing (Linux) or shasum -a 256 -c SHA256SUMS --ignore-missing (macOS).

werkz checks GitHub for a new release once a day, in the background. What happens next depends on how you installed it, and werkz always tells you the best way for your installation: Installed with What happens One-line installer or a downloaded file werkz downloads the new version, verifies it against SHA256SUMS , and replaces itself; restart to use it apt (werkz repository) sudo apt update && sudo apt install --only-upgrade werkz ; with automatic updates on, Ubuntu installs it for you dnf (werkz repository) sudo dnf upgrade werkz A .deb , .rpm , .apk or Arch package file werkz shows the command with the download link for the new package Homebrew brew upgrade --cask werkz A folder werkz can't write to Run the one-line installer again While an update is waiting, the status bar shows ↑ werkz X available , and werkz reminds you when it starts. Type /update to see the exact command (or, for copies that update themselves, to install it right away); werkz --update does the same from a terminal. /update auto off stops automatic installs; werkz still tells you when a new version is out. /update auto on turns them back on. WERKZ_NO_UPDATE=1 disables checks for a session. Builds made with go build without a version (shown as dev ) never check. Only the werkz command is replaced; app icons and launchers stay as installed. Running the one-line installer again also updates everything and keeps your settings.

Ubuntu's background updater installs only Ubuntu's own security updates by default. To let it install new werkz versions too (usually within a day of a release): echo 'Unattended-Upgrade::Origins-Pattern { "origin=werkz"; };' | sudo tee /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/52werkz-unattended Remove that file to turn it off again.

Linux: run uninstall.sh from the release package, or delete ~/.local/bin/werkz , ~/.local/bin/werkz-launch , ~/.local/share/applications/werkz.desktop and the Desktop icon. macOS: delete werkz.app and ~/.local/bin/werkz . Homebrew: brew uninstall --cask werkz . Linux packages: remove the werkz package with your package manager (for example sudo apt remove werkz ). To drop the repository too, delete /etc/apt/sources.list.d/werkz.list and /etc/apt/keyrings/werkz.gpg , or /etc/yum.repos.d/werkz.repo . Your settings and API keys are kept in ~/.config/werkz/ ; delete that folder to remove them too.

Type @ to pick a file or folder; its contents go with your message, so the model doesn't need to read it first. The list follows what you type: @login finds files by name, anywhere in your folders; @src/au/log matches folder by folder ( src/auth/login.ts ). @ alone lists the top level; Tab on a folder opens it ( @src/ ), Enter chooses the highlighted file or folder, Esc closes the list. Enter never sends the message at the same time. In a workspace with several folders, paths start with the folder's name: @api/main.go , @web/src/app.ts . Two folders with the same name are told apart as parent-name . Add lines with @main.go:10-40 , @main.go:10 or @main.go#L10-L40 ; quote paths with spaces: @"My Docs/notes.md" . Mentions are shown as code-style chips in the input box and in the conversation, with a line underneath listing what was attached. Files are attached up to 2,000 lines (100 KB); longer files are cut, and the model can read the rest. A folder sends a two-level listing, and a binary file just its path. The usual rules apply: credential files are never attached, files outside your working folders aren't attached, and an @ inside a word ( me@example.com ) is never a mention. The list uses git's view of the repository (so ignored files don't show up), or a capped scan of a folder that isn't a repository.

Drag over the text you want in the conversation: it's highlighted, and releasing the mouse button copies it. To copy exactly what was written (markdown, or a code block without the frame around it), use Alt+↑ to pick a message, or /copy . A response with code blocks lets you choose one, or press w to save it to a file. werkz copies with your system's clipboard tool ( wl-copy , xclip , xsel , pbcopy , PowerShell on WSL) or, on a Linux desktop without one, with its own small clipboard helper (it keeps your copy pasteable after werkz quits, until you copy something else); inside tmux into tmux's buffer, and over SSH with the OSC 52 terminal sequence. If your terminal doesn't support that, press Ctrl+S and select with the terminal itself.

werkz can read pages and search the web, so it can look up current documentation, an error message or a library's latest version. WebFetch reads any public http(s) page as Markdown, with scripts, menus and page furniture removed. Long pages are read in parts. It needs no setup and doesn't ask: it only reads. Pages on your local network ask first : localhost , private addresses ( 10.x , 192.168.x , …) and cloud metadata addresses. Choose "don't ask again" to allow one host (say, your dev server) for the session. The check is made when connecting, so a public address that redirects or resolves to a local one asks too. WebSearch uses the search built into your model's provider when it has one: Claude (on your Claude model; Anthropic charges $10 per 1,000 searches plus tokens), OpenAI, and Gemini (Google Search). Other models use a search service you set up with /search : /search brave <key> # Brave (free tier) /search tavily <key> # Tavily (free tier) /search searxng <url> # your SearXNG, no key /search # what's used now /search off # no web search Search is allowed in plan mode too: it only reads. /search provider uses only the model's own search; /search auto (the default) prefers it and falls back to a service. Keys can also come from BRAVE_API_KEY , TAVILY_API_KEY and SEARXNG_URL . Everything read from the web reaches the model marked as untrusted: it is told to use it as information and never to follow instructions in it. In Claude Code mode, Claude Code's own web tools are used, with the same rule for local pages.

werkz checks web UI it changes the way you would: it starts the dev server ( DevServer ), opens the page, clicks and types through it, reads the console and the network requests, and compares screenshots from before and after a change. For example: "the signup button does nothing, fix it and check it in the browser". It uses your installed Chrome, Chromium or Edge , with its own separate profile (your bookmarks, logins and cookies are never used). werkz never downloads a browser; if none is installed, the browser tools aren't offered. Set WERKZ_BROWSER to use a particular one. It runs in the background. /browser show opens its window so you can watch (on a desktop), /browser hide goes back, /browser close closes it. /browser shows its state and the running dev servers. The model reads pages through their accessibility tree (the structure screen readers use), with ids it clicks and types by. Screenshots are saved under ~/.cache/werkz/screenshots/ ; comparing two says how much of the page changed and where. Dev servers keep running in the background until stopped, and werkz stops them when you quit or close the terminal. At most four run at once. A page can act on its own after werkz's action has finished, for example a script that starts a download a moment later. werkz shows that in the conversation as it happens ("Browser: the page started a download on its own: report.csv (blocked: downloads are off)"), and tells the model with its next request, so it isn't mistaken for the effect of whatever the model does next. The same goes for popups, navigations and frames werkz blocked and GET forms the page sent. Links that open a new tab or window open in werkz's tab instead (if the site is allowed). Two werkz windows can each use a browser at the same time. If Chrome crashes or you close its window, werkz starts it again when needed.

By default werkz uses its own browser profile, signed in to nothing. To let it work on sites where you are signed in (a staging admin, a dashboard), connect it to the Chrome you already have open: In Chrome, go to chrome://inspect/#remote-debugging and tick Allow remote debugging for this browser instance . You do this once; Chrome remembers it. It needs Chrome 144 or later (Edge, Brave and other browsers built on Chrome have the same page when they are on that version). In werkz, run /browser connect and confirm. Chrome asks Allow remote debugging? : click Allow . That's all: no command to run and no separate profile. If the box isn't ticked yet, /browser connect says so and copies the page's address to your clipboard. werkz finds the Chrome by itself (Chrome, Chromium, Edge, Brave and Vivaldi, on Linux, macOS and Windows); with more than one open, it uses the one you allowed most recently. Chrome asks again each time werkz connects, so nothing connects to your browser without you clicking Allow. To stop allowing it, untick the box (or click Turn off in settings in Chrome's question). Older Chrome, or a Chrome you start yourself Before Chrome 144 the only way was to start Chrome with a debugging port, and Chrome allows that only with a profile of its own (not your default one), so sign in there once to the sites werkz should use. When /browser connect can't find a Chrome that allows it, it also shows this command for your system and copies it. With Google Chrome installed in the usual place it is: Linux: google-chrome --remote-debugging-port=9222 --user-data-dir="$HOME/.config/werkz/chrome-connect" macOS: open -na "Google Chrome" --args --remote-debugging-port=9222 "--user-data-dir=$HOME/Library/Application Support/werkz/chrome-connect" Windows (PowerShell): & "C:\Program Files\Google\Chrome\Application\chrome.exe" --remote-debugging-port=9222 "--user-data-dir=$env:APPDATA\werkz\chrome-connect" Then run /browser connect (or /browser connect 9333 for another port). While connected, a red connected to your Chrome line shows at the bottom. werkz opens one tab of its own and uses only that tab and the popups it opens: it never reads or touches your other tabs, and it never closes Chrome. Sites other than this machine ask first even in bypass; sending forms, uploads and downloads always ask; password and payment fields are never typed into. Downloads it's allowed go where your Chrome saves them. /browser disconnect (or quitting werkz) closes werkz's tab. One limit: Chrome's download setting covers your whole profile, so werkz turns downloads off only while it is acting and for about 1.5 seconds after (your own tabs can't download during that time; watching with /browser view doesn't count as acting); a page werkz opened that starts a download on its own later can save it to your Downloads folder, as any page you open can. Connecting is never saved: each session starts with werkz's own browser.

werkz can use tools from MCP servers: databases, issue trackers, design tools, internal APIs. Add servers in the format Claude Code and Claude Desktop use, either in ~/.config/werkz/mcp.json (yours, in every project) or in .werkz/mcp.json in a project (shared with the team): { "mcpServers": { "github": { "type": "http", "url": "https://api.githubcopilot.com/mcp/" }, "postgres": { "command": "npx", "args": ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-postgres", "${DATABASE_URL}"] }, "files": { "command": "my-mcp-server", "env": { "API_KEY": "${MY_API_KEY}" } } } } A server with command runs on your machine (stdio); one with url is remote (HTTP). ${VAR} and ${VAR:-default} take values from your environment, so keys stay out of the file. Your servers start with werkz. /mcp shows each one's state and number of tools, /mcp tools lists the tools, /mcp disconnect and /mcp connect stop and restart one, and /mcp reload re-reads the files. A project's servers need your approval first. werkz tells you when a project has servers and /mcp shows exactly what each one runs; /mcp approve <name> starts it. The approval is remembered for that project and asked again if the server's command or address changes. Remote servers that need a sign-in say so: /mcp login <name> opens your browser (OAuth), and werkz keeps the tokens in ~/.config/werkz/mcp-auth.json , readable only by you. /mcp logout <name> forgets them. Each tool asks the first time it runs , with "don't ask again" for that tool this session; in auto and bypass mode they don't ask, and in plan mode only tools the server marks read-only run. What a tool returns reaches the model marked as untrusted. The model sees them as mcp__<server>__<tool> .

Every conversation is saved as you go, so you can come back to it. /resume lists the ones from this folder (Tab shows all folders), newest first; type to search what was asked and answered, Enter continues one, Ctrl+X twice deletes one. Continuing a conversation brings back its folders, its model and the whole transcript, and the model picks up where it left off. Files it read before are read again before they're changed. From the command line, werkz -c continues the latest conversation in the current folder and werkz -r opens the list. werkz keeps the latest 500 conversations in ~/.config/werkz/sessions/ , readable only by you. They hold what you and the model wrote, including file contents it read. /resume off stops saving (saved ones stay until you delete them).

OpenRouter gives one key access to hundreds of models. By default werkz shows only its free ( :free ) models. /model switches between every connected provider's models, showing context size and price. /effort sets how much the model thinks before it answers: On Claude the levels are low , medium , high , xhigh and max . Edits are refused if the model hasn't read the file, or if the file changed on disk since it was read. Dialogs ignore keys for a moment after they appear and start on No , so text you're typing can't answer them by accident. Web pages on your local network ( localhost , private and cloud-metadata addresses) are fetched only after you approve, checked again when connecting, so redirects and DNS tricks can't reach them. Your code goes only to the provider you're using. werkz has no server, telemetry or analytics. Prompts and the files the model reads are sent to the model provider you selected (or stay on your machine with Ollama). The Task sub-agent uses the same provider. Saved conversations stay on your machine , in files only your user can read (see Saved conversations ); /resume off stops saving them. @mentions follow the same rules as the Read tool: credential files are never attached and files outside your working folders aren't attached. Keys stay on your machine , in a config file only your user can read (see Configuration ). No surprise spending or sharing: fallback is off unless you turn it on (see Fallback ), Ask mode labels paid models, and model or effort changes that would re-send the conversation uncached warn you first. When a model fails (out of credits, rate-limited, overloaded, offline or erroring), werkz can try another model. Fallback is off by default . Choose your default with /fallback : Mode What happens when a model fails Off (default) The request stops and you decide what to do, for example /model Ask werkz shows the failure and asks which model to switch to: your fallback models (labelled free or paid), any other connected model, or stop. Use it for this message ( Enter ) or the whole session ( Ctrl+A ) Auto werkz switches to the next model in your list without asking (this may use paid models)

Choosing Ask or Auto in /fallback opens a chooser: press Space to add or remove a model; the numbers show the order they're tried. /fallback models edits the list later, and /fallback status shows it. Without a list, werkz uses one model per connected provider, free ones first: Gemini, OpenRouter, Groq, Ollama, then your ChatGPT plan and Claude Code, then Claude, OpenAI, Grok and OpenCode Zen ( /fallback gemini,ollama changes that order).

After switching, werkz stays on the new model for the rest of that message instead of retrying the failing one at every step. Your next message starts with your chosen model again. A provider that's out of credits or has a bad key is skipped for the rest of the session, until /login confirms a working key. With fallback off , werkz never sends your next message to another provider instead. The conversation carries over between providers, so the new model sees everything so far.

By default there is no workspace : werkz works in the folder you start it from. When a task spans several repositories, open a workspace, which is a named set of folders plus optional environment variables. /workspace opens a picker: No workspace (default), your starred and recent workspaces, and + New workspace . In the picker, Ctrl+S stars a workspace, Ctrl+E edits it and Ctrl+X (pressed twice) deletes it. /workspace new asks for a name, the folders (Tab completes paths; the first folder is the main one) and any environment variables, such as APP_ENV=dev . /workspace <name> opens one directly; /workspace none goes back to no workspace. /add-dir <path> adds a folder on the fly. If a workspace is open, the folder is saved into it. /dirs lists the working folders. From the command line: werkz -w my-workspace , or werkz ~/code/api ~/code/web for an unsaved set. Inside a workspace, the model can read, search and edit in every folder, and Grep and Glob search all of them. Shell commands run in the main folder with the workspace's variables. The status bar shows the workspace, for example ▸ my-app (2) . Anything outside the workspace folders still asks first (see Safety and privacy ). To attach a file from one of the folders, start the mention with the folder's name: @api/src/main.go , @web/src/App.tsx . Typing @ lists every folder of the workspace (see Mentioning files ). A workspace's folders also decide which MCP servers start: a project's .werkz/mcp.json is read from the main folder (see MCP servers ).

Every request to a model re-sends the whole conversation, so werkz is designed to keep requests small and cached. Its techniques come from Anthropic's prompt-caching guidance and from how Claude Code, Codex CLI, OpenCode, Gemini CLI, Aider and others manage context. Technique What it does Prompt caching (Claude) The system prompt and tools never change, so every request starts with the same prefix. That prefix and the growing conversation are cached; cache reads cost 0.05× the input price on Opus and Sonnet 5.5 and 0.025× on Fable 5.2. Things that change (folders, date, workspace) are added after the history, so they never break the cache. Cache keep-alive While you're idle, a tiny max_tokens: 0 ping every ~4½ minutes (billed as a cache read) keeps the cache warm for up to 30 minutes. It stops when you switch model, effort or fast mode. Idle warning If the cache has expired and the conversation is 150k+ tokens, werkz suggests /compact before re-sending everything. Compaction /compact (or automatically at 300k tokens) replaces the conversation with a structured summary plus the git state. It waits while a test is failing so the error isn't summarized away, and your newest message is always kept word for word. Context window limit /context window 350k caps the window for every model (the model's own window still applies when it's smaller); /context window full removes the cap. Auto-compaction then runs at ~80% of the window (here ~280k) and never later than 92%, so long sessions re-send less. With Claude Code, the limit is passed on as its auto-compact window (at least 100k). Quiet test output Passing tests and progress lines from go test , vitest, jest, npm test, pytest and cargo test are hidden; failures are kept. Add NO_TRIM=1 to a command to see everything. Big output to a file Command output over 30k characters is cut to its start and end, and the full, untrimmed output is saved to a file the model can search (kept 7 days in ~/.cache/werkz/outputs ). Capped reads and searches Read returns at most 2,000 lines and asks for a range on files over 256 KB. Grep returns file names by default. Cheap sub-agent Broad exploration runs in a separate context on your current provider (Claude Haiku 5.5 at low effort when you're on Claude) and returns only a short report. Project files once AGENTS.md / CLAUDE.md are sent once per session, not with every message. Loop guard Five identical tool calls in a row stop the turn. The status bar shows the cache hit rate . /cache and /cost show tokens read from and written to the cache, money saved, and whether the cache is still warm. /cache ttl 1h switches to the 1-hour cache, and /cache keepalive off turns the keep-alive off. Measured on the live Claude API (Haiku 5.5, three messages): after the first message, each request read 97–99% of its input from the cache and cost about a tenth of the first one.

The status bar shows the session cost: OpenRouter: the cost OpenRouter reports for each request. Claude: estimated from token usage and list prices (including cache reads and writes). OpenAI and xAI: werkz doesn't know their prices, so usage there makes the figure a lower bound, shown as $0.42+? . Anthropic doesn't expose your prepaid credit to an API key, so set your starting credit once with /balance 100 and werkz subtracts its estimate as you work; the Console's Billing page is the exact figure. OpenRouter credit is read live from its API.

Settings live in ~/.config/werkz/config.json (file mode 0600 , readable only by you). Everything in it can be changed from inside werkz, so you rarely need to edit it by hand. Saves are atomic (written to a temporary file, then renamed). If the file ever can't be read (say, after a typo while editing it), werkz tells you, runs with defaults and doesn't overwrite it until you fix it. If two werkz windows are open, the cost they record is added together rather than overwritten. A model chosen with --model applies to that session only; picking one with /model is saved.

Releases are built by GoReleaser ( .goreleaser.yaml ) in GitHub Actions ( .github/workflows/release.yml ): Update VERSION (for example 0.2.0 ), commit and push to main . Tag and push the tag: git tag -a v0.2.0 -m "werkz v0.2.0" && git push origin v0.2.0 The workflow checks that VERSION matches the tag, runs the tests, and publishes the release with a changelog grouped by commit type ( feat: , fix: , docs: ). Each release contains: bare binaries werkz-<version>-{linux,darwin}-{amd64,arm64} (used by the self-updater) werkz-<version>-linux.tar.gz (x86-64 and ARM64, installer, launcher, icons) and werkz-<version>-macos.zip ( werkz.app ), both built by packaging/build.sh as a GoReleaser hook per-platform werkz_<version>_<os>_<arch>.tar.gz archives (used by Homebrew) .deb , .rpm , .apk and Arch Linux packages SHA256SUMS covering all of the above It then rebuilds the signed apt and dnf repositories on the gh-pages branch (served by GitHub Pages at https://tonmoytalukder.github.io/werkz/ ) with packaging/repos/build-repos.sh , keeping only the latest release; pre-releases are skipped. The RPMs and the repository metadata are signed with the werkz GPG key, which the workflow reads from the repository secret SIGNING_KEY (the armored private key). It also updates the Homebrew cask in ZenixBit/homebrew-tap . That needs the repository secret HOMEBREW_TAP_TOKEN : a fine-grained GitHub token with Contents: read and write access to the homebrew-tap repository only. macOS werkz.app : GoReleaser has no format for an app bundle with a Terminal launcher, so build.sh still builds it and GoReleaser attaches the zip. Homebrew users get the plain werkz command. Without GitHub Actions, the same release can be published from a machine with GITHUB_TOKEN=… HOMEBREW_TAP_TOKEN=… goreleaser release --clean . The version is injected at build time with -ldflags "-X main.version=…" ; go install …@vX.Y.Z builds report the module version instead. Installed copies update themselves from releases , so every release must include the bare binaries ( werkz-<version>-<os>-<arch> ) and SHA256SUMS named exactly as they are now, and the tag must be v<version> with a plain MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH version. The updater ( internal/update ) follows /releases/latest , so a release marked as a pre-release or draft isn't offered to users. Copies installed by Homebrew or a Linux package are never replaced (see Updater.Managed ); they get a "update with your package manager" notice instead.

The site at https://tonmoytalukder.github.io/werkz/ is plain static HTML and CSS in site/ (landing page, styles, a small script, self-hosted fonts). tools/sitegen turns it into the published site: it renders docs/*.md into the documentation pages and fills in the documentation list and the release notes, which come from the version tags and their feat: , fix: and build: commits. go run ./tools/sitegen -out _site # build into _site/ python3 -m http.server 8642 --directory _site # preview at http://localhost:8642 .github/workflows/pages.yml publishes it to the gh-pages branch whenever site/ , docs/ or the generator change on main , and after every release (for the new release notes). It never touches the apt/ and rpm/ repositories or the signing key on that branch.

The UI and the agent run in separate goroutines and communicate through messages. The engine owns the conversation; the UI passes it a snapshot of the settings for each turn and changes shared state (permission mode, working folders) only through the engine's synchronized methods. History is stored in a provider-neutral form ( internal/llm ), so a conversation can move between providers. Claude turns also keep the exact API message for faithful replay (thinking blocks, caching). Tests use fake Anthropic and OpenAI-compatible servers ( internal/testutil ); agent.WithProviders lets tests in any package inject them.

Check it: go test -race ./... # tests use fake model servers: no paid API calls golangci-lint run ./... # lint gofmt -l . # formatting (no output means formatted) If you changed what users see, update the matching page in docs/ and, for big changes, the README . The Development guide explains the project layout, how releases are made, and how to preview the website.

Write commit titles in the Conventional Commits style: feat: … for new features, fix: … for bug fixes, docs: … for documentation, build: … for packaging. feat , fix and build titles become the release notes, so write them for users. Keep one change per pull request, and describe what changed and how you tested it. Never commit API keys, tokens, .env files or personal settings. A maintainer reviews every pull request; small, focused changes are reviewed fastest.
